utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, good afternoon, everyone. On the 1st of July, the Trial Chamber fixed this hearing of the evidence of Aleksandar Dimitrijevic to be held by videolink conference. Following the completion of his evidence, the Trial Chamber will review the dead-line for the final briefs in light of the evidence of the witness and the circumstances at the time we do so. It is the illness of the witness which makes it inappropriate for him to travel to The Hague to give evidence. The Trial Chamber, therefore, decided to order the videolink to enable it to hear what he has to say on a number of issues. I wish, first of all, before administering the solemn declaration to clarify with the Belgrade field office where the videolink conference comes from the identity of those present in that room. Can those present please identify themselves to us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good afternoon, Your Honours, my name is Riaz Haider, court officer for the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I think you have beside you Mr. Dimitrijevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Indeed, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there anyone else in the room with you?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I have Dr. Sasa Rafajlovski, and I have someone from the registry with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We were told the doctor would not be there for another 15 minutes or so. That has changed, I take it, and he is now present?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That arrangement was made obviously to ensure the welfare of Mr. Dimitrijevic during the giving of this evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Doctor is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, would you now please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document now being shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We basically cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Haider, there is a problem in the level of sound coming through to the interpreters. Is there anything that can be done about that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That's being looked into, Your Honours, right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Dimitrijevic, we are conscious of your ill health and have no intention of causing distress. We are grateful to you for being there to assist us to try to establish the truth in relation to a number of matters. Arrangements have been made, obviously for the attendance of a doctor in case you should feel the need to consult him. It is for you to tell me if at any stage during this you feel unable to continue and want a break, and we will accommodate that, but our normal schedule would require us to break after 90 minutes in any event. So it is not as if we are going to have lengthy sessions without any interruption. I would now like to proceed to examine you along the lines that the Trial Chamber considers appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: First of all, could you give the Trial Chamber your full name.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Aleksandar Dimitrijevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The 26th of June, 1947.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We know that in 1998 and 1999 you were an officer in the Army of Yugoslavia. Can you tell us, please, when you first enlisted in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear this. We just heard 1965 and not the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I stop you there. We do have a difficulty, and we have to resolve our technical problems with sound levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We're not getting any English interpretation here, just -- the B/C/S is coming through, just -- and there's no English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That may be because the interpreter could hear nothing, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We're on the English channel, the English booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. That part's been resolved, but the -- just hold on, please, Mr. Vasiljevic -- Mr. Dimitrijevic. We have a difficulty in assessing -- in establishing an adequate communication for interpretation purposes. I'll ask you another question, and then we shall -- in fact, I will ask you that question again, and we'll see if in fact there's any improvement. Tell us again, please, when you were first enlisted in the VJ.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: In 1965, I joined the military academy. In 1968, I became an active-duty officer of the then-JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now I have a problem in that I'm getting both languages together. So we solve one problem and create another.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The sound level is still very, very poor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's puzzling about the sound level being poor is that it's very clear for me. Now, if it can be done for us, why can't it be done for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please bear with us, Mr. Dimitrijevic. We are trying to find out how long it will take to put everything into good technical order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, to assist us perhaps I could ask one further question and see if the sound level has improved. Prior to enlisting, were you in higher educational studies; and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from high school in Cuprija, and then I attended the military technical academy in Zagreb from 1965 until 1968.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Which position in the VJ did you occupy in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Up until the 24th of March, 1999, I held the position of chief of the security department of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At any earlier stage in your career prior to the Kosovo troubles, were you involved actively in action as a member of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not quite understand your question. What do you mean "involved actively in action"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, did you ever see action on a front during any of the earlier conflicts in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At any stage in your career have you been decorated or received any order, honour, or award?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you be more --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, while decorations were being given in the JNA; after that, there was a vacuum. When the Army of Yugoslavia was created, there were no more decorations, and no such orders were bestowed upon people. The last one I received sometime in 1988 or perhaps one of those years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you received any decoration of particular significance?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you regard as the highlight of your military career?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the duty I had until I retired because I did everything to help in order for the country to avoid all the horrible things that did happen. Now, it's not for me to say to which extent I succeeded in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When did you retire?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd of March, one day before the bombing. I was told that I was no longer chief of the security administration and that I would be retiring at my own request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And were you effectively retired from that date?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The paper, the decision, on my retirement I actually received within ten days or so; and from that moment onwards, yes, I actively went into retirement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What rank were you at that stage?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: At that stage I was colonel-general of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you had any other jobs since?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The position you held latterly as head of the security administration of the General Staff, we would like to have a little more information about exactly what your responsibilities were; and in giving us that information, it would be helpful if you could distinguish that position from the head of intelligence of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could say to you before that that I did not receive approval from my state, or rather, a decision was not passed, that I have received a waiver in terms of guarding secrets regarding Kosovo and Metohija. However, since in a way some kind of a climate was created that for some reason I did not wish to testify, whereas I do wish to do that, I ask you that we continue; and I'm expressing my good-will in that respect, that I continue answering your questions by way of testimony. However, I do ask you that I be provided with this document, this waiver, by the end of my testimony because I do not want to be prosecuted after this testimony by my very own country for revealing secrets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand what you say, Mr. Dimitrijevic, but let me put your mind at rest. Every document to which I will refer in the course of these questions is now a public document as a result of the cooperation between the authorities of Yugoslavia, various parts of the former Yugoslavia, and this Tribunal. I have no intention of delving into anything that might be regarded as a state secret on which you were forbidden to testify. You should also bear in mind that the subpoena for your attendance here was served upon you through proper channels at the instance of the Government of the Republic of Serbia, and they undertook to provide to us every cooperation in arranging your attendance to give evidence. Any further re-assurance you require, we will take steps to try to provide for you as you request. So I will act upon your request, but I hope I've set your mind at ease to proceed with the evidence along the lines that we intend to pursue, which as I say is simply to explore issues which are already in the public domain in the course of this trial. So could you, therefore, tell us what in 1998 and 1999 were your principal responsibilities in that post and how that role differed from the head of intelligence.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The security administration, or rather, the counter-intelligence service consisted at that time of four departments, that is to say the level of the security administration we had the operative department, the analysis department, the general department, and we also had a military police department. In actual fact, at that time the military police in terms of its professional nature was linked to the security administration; and as for the professional use of the military police, the security administration always had to provide its view on that. As for the main tasks of the security administration, at that time this is what they were. First of all, it was counter-intelligence activity, or rather, protecting the Army of Yugoslavia, its members, its facilities and installations from intelligence and other subversive activity that would come from elsewhere, from foreign countries; furthermore, protection from terrorism, that is to say everything in relation to that; and finally, protection, or rather, discovering, following, documenting, and putting a stop to activities of organized crime that would jeopardize the army, the members of the military, and its facilities and installations. The difference between the security administration and the intelligence administration was in the following: In terms of its duties, the security administration was supposed to carry out intelligence activities outside the country, abroad. Practically, it did not have any authority to work within the country in collecting information about the activities of foreign armed forces and others that were relevant at that time in terms of commanding the army as a whole, as we all know what was going on then. Every now and then, sporadically there were clashes because operatives and intelligence services tried to carry out some duties within the country and establish some contacts, which was not in accordance with the powers vested in that administration. So basically, the security administration was in charge of security, if one can put it that way, internally, within the country in terms of all attacks that may be launched against the military, whereas the intelligence department was supposed to work abroad and protect the army from external activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I think there is one error in the transcript following that answer. You have been recorded as saying the security administration was supposed to carry out intelligence activities outside the country, abroad. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: No, it was a mistake by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, obviously it was a mistake in interpretation. That was the task of the intelligence service, the intelligence administration; it was their duty to collect information outside the country, whereas the security administration was supposed to work against all activities against the army within the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. Just one other matter arising out of your answer. You said that you have a military -- you had a military police department. Can I take it that the security administration was also responsible for dealing with routine criminal activity within the VJ?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Within the administration, as I have already mentioned, there was a department for the military police. The responsibility of that department was equipping, training, everything that would mean logistics so that the military police units would be trained and equipped to carry out their duties, equipped properly, and so on. As for the use of military police units, that was exclusively within the domain of the commander's decisions. They would decide when they would use military police units, whereas our duty and obligation was, as I said, that they should be trained and equipped to carry out their specific tasks: Regulating traffic, general security measures, all the way up to those tasks that all police forces in the world do, more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you have any responsibilities at all in relation to the military justice system?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, none whatsoever. Quite simply, whatever was supposed to be done by way of prosecuting, say, military police and other departments before this is handed over to the judiciary, then we were still in charge; but once we handed them over to them, then our authority would cease.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was simply curious to know whether you had anything at all to do with logistics in relation to the military justice system; in other words, seeing that they had offices, equipment, and personnel, or was that nothing whatsoever to do with you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, this had nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I now want to ask you about a number of individual people. I will be asking you about others through this examination, but I just want to be clear about your relationship with a number of these and your knowledge of their activities before we proceed. Could you tell us, first of all, who was Aleksandar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Aleksandar Vasiljevic was a general who was head of the security administration up until 1992, I think; then he retired. Later on, I found out from the media that he was re-activated during 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was that after you had been retired?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: John Crosland, who was he?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: During those years, he was the British military attache in Yugoslavia, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, he has provided the Trial Chamber with information, some of which you might at first sight think was confidential but has been openly disclosed information. So again, we are simply exploring matters which have already been aired before the Trial Chamber. What was your relationship, your personal relationship, first of all, with him? How did you get on with him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you, Mr. President, that I did not have any personal relationships with any one of the military attaches. We did not socialise outside working hours. We did not visit. We were not family friends. Our families didn't know each other. We did not have any informal contacts, as it were. In all fairness, we did meet at various receptions, but all our conversations were of an official nature, and for the most part they were conducted on the official premises of the Office For Liaising With Foreign Missions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In what circumstances did you meet with him professionally?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, contacts with military diplomatic representatives on the part of the representatives of the Army of Yugoslavia were carried out in accordance with the official regulations through the liaison office with foreign missions. So if any of the military envoys or attaches of representatives of any country whatsoever wanted to be received by the Chief of the General Staff or to meet with any of the generals, officers of the Army of Yugoslavia, that person had to submit this request to the liaison office, and then it would be relayed to whoever the addressee was. And then the decision was made whether to accept the request or to reject it, and then contacts would follow, only then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who is Momir Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Momir Stojanovic was at that time a lieutenant-colonel, I believe. He was the chief of the Pristina Corps section -- the security section of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Branko Gajic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Branko Gajic was a colonel at the time in the Army of Yugoslavia. He was first the chief of the operations department, and then he became my deputy in the security administration. So he was the man that I worked with very closely on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then four who have no obvious link with the VJ. First of all, Milomir Minic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Comrade or Mr. Milomir Minic, I may have met him in those years maybe twice or three times, not more than that, at some receptions for the independence day, the national holidays, and so on. And in 1998, I think that we may have met four or five times at various meetings organized by the then-president, Mr. Milosevic. I do know that he was an official of the Socialist Party of Serbia and that he was a high-ranking official, but I did not really communicate with him at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Dusan Matkovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: As for Dusan Matkovic, I know him from the media as an official of the Socialist Party of Serbia. The first time that I met him face-to-face was at a meeting in President Milosevic's office, and we may have met three, four, or five times. You will allow me this hesitation because ten years have passed, so I can't remember whether it was three, four, or five times. I couldn't be more specific than that, but you will accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Zoran Andjelkovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zoran Andjelkovic - Baki, that was his nickname - the first time that I was formally introduced to him was at a meeting with President Milosevic, and we saw each other at those few meetings that were held in the -- in July and August 1998. I believe that was the time-period. That's where we would meet. After that, I left. They went their own way, whatever it is that they did; and after that time-period, I did not have any contacts with him. We did not communicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And lastly, Nikola Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Nikola Sainovic was the deputy prime minister in the federal government at that time, and as the other three he was a high-ranking official in the Socialist Party of Serbia. He may even have been the deputy president of the Socialist Party of Serbia. I met him on a couple of occasions when there was an issue of the funding for the army, and the previous prime minister Radoje Kontic convened some meetings to deal with this problem of the funding for the army, and he would attend those meetings. And in 1998, we saw each other at the meetings that I've just described at President Milosevic's place, and of course I met him at various receptions held to celebrate national holidays, and we would exchange a few words. So I never really did socialise with him or anything of the sort. I know -- what I know about him is what I believe most of the citizens of our country know, not more than that. And I remember him as a man who in 1998 as the deputy prime minister in the federal government went to Kosovo to carry out certain tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When in relation to each of these last four you say that you met them on a number of occasions in 1998, is it the case that the first time you met them you met all of them together along with others at one meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose, yes. Well, it was at a meeting, definitely. It was definitely not outside of any official meetings, but I can't really recall when it was. I cannot recall the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give us a little more information, then, about who apart from them and you attended the meetings at -- generally speaking, at which you met them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have to say that that year, in this time-period, there were quite a few meetings held in -- at Mr. President Milosevic's place involving various participants, and I attended quite a few of those meetings. When we're talking about those persons that you've just mentioned, I can say that -- I think it was four or five times. I cannot really be more specific than that. And now, as to who attended those meetings, the meetings that they attended, the army was represented by the Chief of the General Staff, General Perisic; the commander of the 3rd Army, General Dusan Samardzic, Colonel-General Dusan Samardzic; I think that General Pavkovic attended all those meetings, maybe apart from one. As for the MUP, the representatives were the minister, Vlajko Stojiljkovic; Generals Djordjevic, Obradovic, and Lukic; it appears to me they attended all the meetings. Sometimes there was also the -- sometimes it was also President Milutinovic. I don't think that he was there on all occasions. And the gentlemen that you asked me about, Sainovic, Matkovic, Minic, and Andjelkovic, and myself, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did all of these meetings involve President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There would not have been those meetings if he hadn't been there. I suppose he organized those meetings, convened them, and he chaired them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where were they held?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that all of those meetings were held in the room that was called the library in Beli Dvor, the official premises, the official residence where President Milosevic moved in as soon as he was elected the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what period of time to the best of your recollection are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can recall now, since I was not told what I would be testifying about, but to the best of my recollection I think it was in July and August 1998, maybe some 10 or 15 days before that time-period and perhaps a couple of days later. Let's say until September and maybe even into October. But the -- most of them were held in July and August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was there a common theme?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the theme that was discussed at those meetings -- well, except for one where some other themes were also discussed, but the issue discussed was the situation in Kosovo and Metohija and how to resolve that problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can you remember whether there was some significant item on the initial agenda at the very beginning of this exercise in relation to controlling the situation in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you would be so kind and be more specific because I didn't quite understand. Items that was in common: Do you mean some introductory remarks or something like that? Well, could you please be more specific, and then I'll answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm trying to establish whether you recollect that there was a particular reason for getting this group of people together apart from simply to discuss the problem of Kosovo, whether it was some particular way of dealing with it that was an issue.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that there was any special way. When we're talking about the civilians, they probably saw President Milosevic much more frequently. On some occasions before the meetings started, when we from the army would come, they would already be there, and they had obviously been dealing with some issues with President Milosevic, or they would stay on after we left to discuss some other issues. I cannot tell you about that because I did not participate in that. But once President Milosevic opened the meeting, then the only item on the agenda would be the situation in Kosovo. And I failed to mention that General Susic, chief of President Milosevic's military cabinet, was also present there - I forgot to mention that - at all those meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One account we have before us in this case is that the result of the meeting - and this is the first of these meetings, which is probably the same as you're talking about - the result of the meeting was to start with realization of the plan for fighting terrorism in Kosovo. Does that help you to remember what was the purpose of getting this group of people together?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I've already said that the purpose always was to get an assessment of the situation and measures that should be taken in Kosovo and Metohija. So I do remember that at the first of those meetings - I can't really tell you when it was, the date - we were told that a plan should be put together, and it might be the case that we came to the first meeting and that General Pavkovic had already drafted that plan. But it would be a more likely scenario that this task was issued at the meeting, that he should put together a plan for dealing with terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija. And then once he drafted this plan, he reported this about the concept that he had in his head as the commander of the Pristina Corps, and then everything just followed after that and went in this direction. Why General Pavkovic? I was present, or rather, I participated in a conversation at President Milosevic's place when he called the Chief of the General Staff and myself to discuss just one issue. It happened sometime in late May or perhaps mid- or late June. President Milosevic had this idea to appoint General Pavkovic the commander of all the forces in Kosovo and Metohija, to appoint him commander of all the military and MUP forces there. General Perisic and myself opposed this idea, and our justification was that it would be a bad solution both for the military and for the MUP for a very simple reason, because there would probably be obstruction and refusal on the part of the MUP to subordinate its units to General Pavkovic's command. So since this didn't work out, and I think that it was in early June, it was at a later stage -- well, Milosevic accepted our suggestion and this meeting ended on that note. After that, I think it was perhaps in the second half of June - I believe that's when the first of those meetings was held - and President Milosevic in the presence of this same group of people ordered that a plan be put together for the solution of the problem of terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija. But if I remember correctly, that particular meeting at Milosevic's place I think was preceded by another meeting of the Supreme Defence Council, where the Chief of the General Staff presented the assessment of the situation in Kosovo and Metohija and made some proposals as to how those problems should be solved. And I think that a political decision was made at that meeting or a military decision because the Supreme Defence Council was the highest organ that was in control of the army, so a decision was made to draft a plan and to start solving the terrorist problem in Kosovo. I may be a little bit too broad in my explanations, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now you -- in the beginning of that answer you referred to being at a meeting with Milosevic and General Pavkovic at which the question of Pavkovic commanding all forces in Kosovo was raised. Who --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, that's not what I said. I said that I attended this meeting with General Perisic, the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're quite right, Mr. Dimitrijevic. It's my mistake. Now, the account I gave you a moment ago of recollection of the purpose of the meetings was a quote from -- of something said by General Pavkovic, and he puts the first of these meetings at which there were a large number present as the 30th of May, 1998, which would suggest that the meeting with Perisic and Milosevic was possibly earlier than that. Is -- does that fit with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure, Mr. President. I would put this meeting in the period between the 30th of May and the 10th of June. Why do I say the 10th of June? Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now -- yes, carry on.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Because as I followed this trial in the media, I recollect that on the 10th of June the Main Board of the Socialist Party of Serbia made the decision that a certain number of persons, in particular those that you mentioned, should be sent to Kosovo to solve various problems involving the refugees, the health service, the economy, and so on. So it somehow stuck in my mind that it may have been before this meeting and after this conversation, but I really can't be very definite about that given the time lapse. So it may have happened after that, but I would, rather, put this meeting sometime in the period between the 1st and the 10th of June, but I cannot claim that with 100 per cent certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dimitrijevic, the name Joint Command has been associated with these meetings. Is that a name or title that you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that this name came into being later. At the time when those meetings were held, that name did not exist. If it was mentioned sporadically as the Joint Command, the MUP and the disciplinary team, the coordination team, those terms were used -- a number of different terms, in fact, for this command, if I may call it that. So I never really addressed this. I never really sought any explanations because in military terms this was something that was completely unacceptable to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I stop you there. It's important, bearing in mind, also, your own condition of health, that we try to have answers as directly to the point as possible. I don't want to stop you where you feel an explanation is necessary, but my simple question is whether you were familiar with this name Joint Command, and I don't think you're really addressing that question. You're addressing what a command is. Like so many others before you, you're so defensive about this name. I just want to know if it means anything to you, you recollect anything about it.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I have no reason to be defensive, but at those meetings this name was hardly ever mentioned. It is my impression that at a later stage it was supposed to serve somebody's purposes, and by that I mean General Pavkovic, to cover some of his activities so that he could say, I have the Joint Command behind me. To my knowledge, this Joint Command was never established, and I was never told about the existence of this command that would purportedly exercise command because what else would it do apart from that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why, then, did the thinking of Milosevic leap from let's put Pavkovic in control of everybody to let's have a great big committee that discusses and deals with anti-terrorist activities in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that you could really establish this link between those two things. If I recall correctly, sometime in March 1998 the State Security Service carried out an action in the village of Drenica, it was in Gornji Prekaz where several dozens -- dozen of persons were killed. And after that, the MUP was given a task, to prevent the rampaging of the terrorist gangs who went out on to the roads, robbed people, checked their IDs. But it was apparent that all of those measures were not sufficient, and I assume - and this is nothing else; this is just my assumption - that a coordination should be set up so that the tasks should be issued to the army by the supreme commander, who was also the head of the Supreme Defence Council, and that the same -- those same orders would be relayed through the minister of the interior to the MUP organs because it was quite obvious; it was a fact at that time that it would be very difficult for anyone else to issue any tasks to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, just two or three more questions on this topic. You mentioned Mr. Milutinovic as being present. Have you a clear recollection of his presence at any of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is difficult for me to give you a specific answer because President Milutinovic, as the president of Serbia, before Milosevic was elected the president of Yugoslavia, chaired some meetings. So now I can't really distinguish between the two, the meetings in the Serbian Presidency building or -- and the meetings in Beli Dvor, so I can't really be very sure about that. But if he attended those meetings, he did not attend all of them. I'm sure about that. But after -- now that you've asked me this, I can't really be very certain whether he attended any of those meetings at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does the name Operations Inter-Departmental Staff For the Suppression of Terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No. No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think I'm right in saying that --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I do apologise. As for that name, I really don't know what would fall under that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the court deputy there would put in front of you our Exhibit P2166. Now, you'll see that that bears to be minutes of a meeting under that title held in the Beli Dvor palace in October 1998 at which you are recorded as being present and which was chaired by Milosevic and attended, among others, by Mr. Milutinovic and generally by the personnel you've referred to as being at the other meetings.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this paper is something that I see for the very first time, absolutely. The first thing that I wish to say in relation to these meetings as regards this document is the following: There weren't any stenographic notes kept at these meetings or minutes, either. Since I usually sat somewhere near General Susic, the chief of the military cabinet, and I see now that he is the signatory of this record, that he compiled it, I must say that I am completely taken by surprise. I see that the record consists of 16 pages. Now, when this was done and on the basis of which information he wrote this record, I really cannot say. However, what I find striking at this very instant is the conclusion that I read just now where it says: "At the end of the meeting of the Operative Inter-Departmental Staff For the Suppression of Terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija," so I had never heard that name then, "the president of the FR of Yugoslavia Slobodan Milosevic proposed and the staff unanimously accepted the following conclusions." The presented assessments are being adopted from the statements made by Generals Pavkovic; General Lukic; the president of the Council of Citizens of the Assembly, Milomir Minic; and the last one is to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the text. It was very fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- delimit the border belt towards Macedonia. I have to tell you in all fairness that I could not have imagined that anything like this existed on paper. To write that at the very end of the meeting President Milosevic proposed and that the staff unanimously adopted conclusions, I think that that absolutely does not correspond to the truth for a simple reason: Milosevic did not make proposals. He made decisions, and others could make proposals. On the basis of this, it seems that he proposed conclusions and that the staff, as Susic calls it, adopted the -- his proposal, his proposed conclusions, rather. As far as I'm concerned -- well, I assume there is not enough time for me to read all these 16 pages, but at any rate the first thing that strikes me here is that this is something that does not correspond to the truth or to my recollection, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Another thing, if I may. Perhaps if this were to be read up -- well, if there is this record, then there are probably records or transcripts from other meetings too. Perhaps that could be analysed, and it could then be concluded with full reliability whether it was written at the time or later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would be quite happy if the court deputy gave you that document at the break --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- at the break we will have and allow you to read it in the half-hour or so that will be available, and then you would have an opportunity to make any other comments you wish to make on it. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just in relation to the transcript, page 25, line 8: [In English] "... at the time or later on," [Interpretation] ... for who knows what reasons. That is what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just give me one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is the only document that looks official in relation to meetings of this nature, so there aren't others, Mr. Dimitrijevic, of this nature with which to compare it. And I think just one other -- one final question on this theme. The anti-terrorist activity that was the subject of these earlier meetings, can you recollect that there was a plan to address the problem in stages and that there was a title for at least some of the stages of that plan?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I remember correctly, since at the Supreme Defence Council a decision was made to the effect that a comprehensive assessment should be made as well as a plan for dealing with terrorism, I think that after that -- I think it was the beginning of June, actually, 1998. I think that after that, the Chief of General Staff ordered that such a plan be made. You said that there was no information involved that are a state secret or a military secret and that I can freely speak. I think that the name of the plan was Grom, thunder. A plan was made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're aware of that name, so you can speak about it freely.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the task was to make a plan if there were to be an escalation in Kosovo in order to forestall such an escalation so that there would not be a spillover of activities to the rest of the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This plan was actually something that I saw often in literature in the west. It was a contingency plan. That's what it's called. It contained -- or rather, it consisted of two stages, two stages. The first stage -- or rather, tasks are given to the strategic groups, to the armies, to the command of the navy; and the first stage involved that absolutely all activities should be carried out in terms of guarding the border, protecting the border; then protecting units, commands, facilities, members of the army, vehicles when travelling, and so on. So in this plan, this was the first stage for all the strategic groups. I have to say that in the security administration when we would work on paper on the work of the security administration, and that involved various tasks, in the security administration when all these things were done my deputy, then-Colonel Gajic, went to these meetings. If I remember correctly, the second stage entailed the use of units for eliminating and suppressing terrorist groups, but I think that what was written everywhere was only on the order of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. So if I can put it this way, no one would -- could assess on his own bat that that would be the right time to use the unit. The order had to come from the very top, from the Chief of General Staff, or rather, the General Staff and, of course, that is what he gets from the Supreme Defence Council. So this second stage involved that, and this second stage related to a period of, say, 15 or 20 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dimitrijevic, what -- to what extent did the plan for combatting terrorism involve the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, our plan, that is to say the plan that was elaborated in the General Staff and that was entrusted to the General Staff by the Supreme Defence Council, went down the chain of command to the strategic groups, and they further conveyed this to their subordinates, that is to say to the corps; and every army, every strategic group, made its own plan on the basis of that plan, and then the corps would make its own plan, and then every brigade would make its own plan and so on and so forth. In this plan as far as the MUP was concerned, what was invariably present was there, that is to say effect cooperation with the MUP in terms of controlling territory and all the other tasks where the MUP was supposed to be engaged. Actually, in the General Staff we firmly advocated the view that as far as terrorism in Kosovo is concerned it had to be resolved through anti-terrorist actions that were to be carried out by the MUP and that the army was only supposed to do what the constitution said; namely, protecting the border, commanding units, personnel, and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I now want to turn to certain things that we already have before us reflecting statements you have made at various times in 1998 and 1999, and I would like you to look first of all at the exhibit we have, 3D664. Now, just look at the outside page of that, first of all, and tell me if you recognise that document in general terms. Is that the sort of a document of a type that you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: This document was made and submitted only to the Chief of General Staff. I must tell you that I have never seen it before in this form. Even that is not the entire truth. I saw it in some book that came out after the year 2000. I think its title was "Military Secret," and allegedly it published parts of collegium meetings that were held. So this first part, this formal part - if I can put it that way - that is something I have never seen before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it consistent with your understanding that the meetings of the collegium of the Chief of the General Staff were recorded and that minutes were compiled from these recordings?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Meetings were recorded and then the office, the cabinet, of the Chief of General Staff had the task of putting these statements on paper, and then it would be archived as documentation of the collegiums that were held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, in this one, if you look for your own name, you'll see more than two pages recording things that you said. And if you go about two-thirds of the way through the passages that relate to you, you'll see that one of the things you were saying to the meeting was that it would take time for the OSCE Verification Mission to become fully operational and that this would be advantageous to the KLA. Is that an accurate reflection of something you said regularly at meetings of the collegium?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to skim through this, and this does look like the way in which I addressed the collegium and how I presented the problems that were within the domain of my work, if I can put it that way. Since we are talking about the 6th of November here, 1998, that is to say after those night-time negotiations, if I can put it that way, and this solution that was finally found between Milosevic and Holbrooke with great difficulty. So then the situation -- this is the situation ten days after that. During these talks that Milosevic had with Holbrooke that night, I think it was the 24th, the night between the 24th and 25th of October, 1998 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I didn't really want to create any problem here. I was hoping that I was simply summarizing something that you felt quite strongly about and mentioned a number of times at meetings, that the OSCE would take time to get up and running and that that, in fact, did -- not only would it give an opportunity to the KLA to regroup but it did in fact give an opportunity to the KLA to regroup. Now, is that stating it too simply?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: You are absolutely right. That is what I was saying. That's why I wanted to say it. When negotiations took place that night on the withdrawal of the units that were in the area into barracks, my fear was that as the units of the Army of Yugoslavia withdrew into barracks, as the territory was abandoned, this would most certainly cause the return of terrorists to these areas because regardless of some of the assurances made by civilians that terrorism had been eradicated, that was simply not the case. They were simply dispersed in the woods, so it is correct. When we found out that inter alia Milosevic had agreed that a verification mission should come in, we already had some operative information at the time that this mission would not be completed very quickly because that was not in the interest of those who had offered it in the first place. Time will show that I was right at the time. If I can remember correctly, it was supposed to consist of 2.000 people instantaneously, and it never reached that personnel level, not even after several months. I think the maximum personnel level was 1.200 or 1.500 people. Indeed -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, we've been told that it was even worse than that, that the KLA were not signatories to any of the agreements which were entered into, and therefore, there was nothing that anyone could do to hold them to the state of status quo that the agreements were designed to establish.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I really don't know whether the KLA was the signatory of any agreement, but I know for sure that many activities of the KLA were well-known in the west to people who were involved in all of this, that a lot of assistance was coming from the outside, training as well. After all, at that time through the mission, through various humanitarian, non-governmental organizations we knew that the KLA was assisted financially and that weapons were being provided to them in order to have them armed and so on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me stop you there because we have a great deal of information about that. Was there a general feeling among officers at your level in the VJ that the agreements that had been entered into were unfair to the VJ and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's possible. I don't know. I know that as far as the agreement was concerned, to accept the verification mission of the OSCE, that we found out about that agreement only some ten days after the negotiations were over, we in the military, that is. So what was agreed, all the things that were agreed, and what were all the contents of the agreement that was signed I really cannot say because I was not made aware of any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you obviously knew enough to be able to say that you were going to be presented with a growing problem because of the KLA filling the vacuum that was created by the withdrawal of your forces.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President. I don't know what the talks, negotiations, were formally; but I know what was happening on the ground, and we cautioned about that all the time. I personally issued warnings many times to the effect that we would have a serious problem. We as a service then had information to the effect that somewhere in Switzerland a decision had been made to wait for the spring in order to start a general uprising. Everything that happened after the signing of the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement went in that direction. They were being trained; they were being armed; training centres functioned in Albania; weapons were being into Kosovo in a variety of ways; instructors were coming in; I remember that there were people from Iran there and people from the west who sat with them, helped them, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Let me --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: So all of this was done --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me then -- we'll have a break then in a moment, but just before we do that let me ask you to look at one more of these documents, which is 3D557, and in the English it's page 19 of that. You go -- almost towards the end of the document. It's very long. It's 21 pages in English. If you go to fairly near the end, the third-last page, there's an entry where you say something about personnel carriers.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let me have a look. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: This is the collegium that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you're making a point about the MUP being given personnel carriers that were the property of the military police battalion, so therefore logistical matter for which you are responsible. Now, what was it that was concerning you at that stage?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, when you say "responsible," I as head of the security administration did not have the right to give anyone any resource from the battalion of the military police to anyone else. This could only be done by the commander under whose command the said battalion of the military police was. What was all of this about? After the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement, after the insistence that all units be returned to their garrisons, buildings, except for three that remained in the area, that all the technical equipment that was given to the MUP for their use be returned to the army, my concern was since the MUP were dragging their feet on this, that this indeed be returned because our units, that is to say without the military police battalion and 20 APCs, that is a considerable weakening. So we really had to have that in the arms control agreement as military equipment, equipment in the hands of the military, not of the MUP. That's what I'm talking about, and I see that the same goes for helicopters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What actually happened?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: It was supposed to be returned to the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: And they were not supposed to be in the hands of the MUP, this equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was the equipment returned to the army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think it was, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was it recorded as being in the hands of the army or the hands of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, even though I really want to give you an answer, I cannot give you an answer to that question. This equipment was dealt with with the operations department and the logistics department. They were keeping tabs on that, so I really don't know where and how it was presented. I assume that from the point of view of the law it could not be in the hands of the MUP but, rather, in the hands of the military. But I really don't have any specific knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just to complete this, would you look, please, at P924, and in this instance it's an even longer document. In English, the section I'm looking at is a bit beyond the middle. It's page 26 in English, and it's where General Ojdanic is speaking, and he refers to General Clark. The part I'm interested in is at the top of page 26 in English, if that helps to identify it, where it starts: "Clark literally said the following ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's in the middle of page -- page number 24 of the B/C/S hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So middle of page 24, please, in your copy. And the reference to: "Clark literally said the following ..." Now, just read that -- the rest of that paragraph to yourself --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just read it to yourself, and then tell me whether this is General Ojdanic dealing with exactly the same point. It may be you've already read past the part that matters --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what General Ojdanic appears to be saying is that Clark had asked why the VJ had not fulfilled the demands from the agreement to withdraw all heavy equipment that had been given to the MUP. Now, is that a reference to the same problem?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Since he mentions General Clark, this is what was concluded as part of the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement that was reached in October 1998. So the equipment was not returned, and that's what he's talking about here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this is a discussion on a meeting on the 24th of December, 1998. Had General Ojdanic continued after reaching agreement with Clark to meet Clark on any other occasion or discuss things with him on any other occasion?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, when talks were held in October by Milosevic and Holbrooke and we in the General Staff, the Chief of the General Staff and his team were involved in talks with General Clark and his team, General Ojdanic did not attend those talks as far as I can remember. Now, as to whether he met with him, I don't know about that. I'm not aware of it, but it appears to me that on the 24th of December he did speak to him on the phone, and what he recounted for us was what transpired, what had transpired during the course of that telephone conversation, and this concerned that the heavy equipment that remained in the MUP hands could be misused and that the results of this misuse could then be blamed on the army. And if I recall it correctly, sometime in January or February 1999 General Ojdanic, again, at a collegium meeting, recounted his conversation with General Clark. And if I remember correctly, I think that he said that that conversation was also attended by General Krga, who was the chief of the intelligence administration, and this was, again, a telephone conversation. So this is all I know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dimitrijevic. We will now have a break for half an hour. We'll resume at 25 minutes past 4.00, and meanwhile, please relax and make yourself more comfortable. And if you do have time to read that other document, we could return to that when we resume at 4.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, we're now ready to resume. Have you had an opportunity of looking a bit more closely at that document which we have numbered P2166?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether it looks genuine to you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, as far as the stamp and the signature are concerned, it does look like an original; but as far as the contents of this document are concerned, I did not attend any such meeting. And after all, my first question, my first remark -- the last note here, I quote, is "no shorthand notes were kept." I would like to know, although this is outside of my purview, how could the person compiling the minutes - and this is General Susic - how was he able to memorise all those details and there were no shorthand notes and I never saw him keep any records or notes in any way. As far as the contents of this document are concerned, this looks to me like a paper that was supposed to serve a purpose but to be a compilation of everything that was said at all of those five or six meetings. What is not logical in this document, so we're talking about the Serbian version at page 3 where General Pavkovic has the floor, and he actually presents a report about the implementation of the plan, and at page 3, he says: "The declaration of the state of emergency was not acceptable for several reasons. First, we would have caused the response of the external factor," and so on. "Secondly, that would call for the mobilisation of the wartime units and so on." And the third reason -- I do apologise to the interpreters. So the first would be the response of the external factor, the foreign factors who would intervene militarily; secondly, this would call for the mobilisation of wartime units, and as indicated here that would cause distress among the people in Serbia; the third reason, the use of stronger forces to fight the terrorists would draw the attention of the domestic and international public. And now we come to a part which is completely incomprehensible to me in light of the fact that there would be quite a few casualties on the terrorist side but also among our own forces. So we're talking about the plan to combat terrorism, and here we explain -- we're explaining why the state of emergency was not declared. And the last thing here, it says: "Our plan was not to kill all Siptars" -- well, I never heard anyone say that, to put it in those terms, or to expel them from Kosovo and Metohija. So, Mr. President, this looks to me like a document that was made in accordance with some plan that was to be used to cover some things. I have no other way of describing it, and then General Pavkovic goes on to brief those present. And when he says about the effects of the implementation of the plan, he says the following: "The mass importation of military equipment and weapons from Albania was stopped and the infiltration of the terrorist forces." So at that time, this was stopped en masse, but it was never stopped definitely. Under item 2, the escalation of terrorism was stopped; the promotion of the so-called KLA was stopped. Unfortunately, all of those items appeared on the agenda at a later stage and so on and so forth. The next thing that drew my attention. In front -- talking about the villages that were disarmed, the consumption of ammunition and all those other details, talking about all those things in front of President Milosevic, well, this never happened while I was there, telling him how much ammunition was consumed calibre by calibre, how much fuel was consumed. I don't know of any instance of this kind of detail being explained to him. I can see here that in item 12 it says -- it is the assessment of the Joint Command. I don't really recall if this term was used and what this Joint Command was, and I can tell you why I asked this question as I go on in my analysis of this document. And then we have the briefing or the report by Major-General Sreten Lukic, and this is where I come across the first great contradiction, and he says: "In the execution of the tasks," he talks about the tasks that were executed, "the control and protection of the roads and their liberation from the assaults by terrorist groups. "2. Reinforcement and protection of the areas that are not covered by terrorist" -- "where there is no terrorist activity. "3. Protecting the towns of Pec, Prizren, and Mitrovica. "4. Training the reserve force of the police." Mr. President, so after all this the question that I ask is, how could the MUP carry out any anti-terrorist activities in Kosovo? What kind of such activities they carried out when we have General Lukic presenting this report on behalf of the MUP, and he's talking about the tasks that were carried out. Pavkovic talked about the tasks that were carried out, and the plan was for the army to secure the border - I already talked about that - and for the MUP to carry out counter-terrorist actions and to deal with the problem of terrorism. At the next page in the Serbian version, that's page 8, the president of the Chamber of Citizens, Mr. Minic, says that the terrorist forces had been defeated and that they cannot be consolidated again. Unfortunately, he was proven wrong quite soon as time went by, and then he says in paragraph 3 the terrorists were defeated but not completely destroyed. And in item 7, it says that no -- there are no major terrorist forces in Kosovo, only remnants of those groups, which is of course not true. But given that Minic is a civilian, obviously unacquainted with the military issues, I don't really want to criticise him because he couldn't really know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We have your --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I do have some more remarks which are quite important, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you can make these as briefly as possible, please, because we have many things to deal with.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Well, the last thing that I want to comment on, the commander of the Pristina Corps General Pavkovic then goes on to note the tasks that should be implemented in the forthcoming period, and he says under 1: "Assist the OSCE verification mission; 2" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- "with the increased security at the state border through line and indepth security," and so on and so forth. So first we're talking about things that were done. Nobody says that actually he did that, or it's not specified who did that, but -- and now we're talking about securing the state border and all those other things. So all in all -- or for instance, the 3rd Army commander, General Samardzic, at the next page says in item 2: "Analyse the possibility of keeping three military units in Kosovo for three weeks after the completion of achievement of the agreement." Why would General Samardzic make this proposal when in accordance with an agreement with General Clark those units were there and he knew that because those were his units? So there are quite a few things here that indicate to me together with this conclusion that the president proposes and the staff accepts those conclusions, this is an indication that this paper was not done at the meeting because I can't recall any meeting that proceeded in this manner where all those things that are listed here were actually said. I think that this paper was simply drafted at a later stage for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me just clarify a couple of things about that with you. Information before the Trial Chamber coming from General Pavkovic indicates a plan comprising four stages, one of which was equipping and mobilising units of the MUP and deblocking Kijevo village in Malisevo municipality; the second stage was restoring communications in Kosovo in five to seven days through the use of both the MUP and VJ forces in taking over selected facilities and points; the third was disarming terrorist groups in Kosovo in nine to ten days; and the fourth was manoeuvring units of the MUP to secure and control the territory in eight to ten days. Now, that suggests activity of the VJ other than simply in the border belt, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, from what you say, that would follow, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the other thing I'd like you just to look at briefly, and we will move on. If you look at P1011. This is an extract from Vojska. Is it just one page that you have? And you'll see that that contains some of the figures, the detailed figures about refugees that match the figures in the operations inter-departmental staff minutes. Do you see that? In other words, they match figures that are attributed in the minutes to General Pavkovic's report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's page 72 in the English.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: May I just ask you what is the date for this issue of Odbrana or Vojska, whatever the publication is. What date was it published? When was this published, Mr. President, if I may ask?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This was published in 2001, but you'll see that it refers to the report and conclusions on the implementation of the plan for stamping out terrorism.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what do you understand Vojska to be?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I did not understand your question. What do you mean when you say what was Vojska?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: It's the armed force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but do you know of a publication by the same name?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I do apologise. You're referring to the journal Vojska. Yes, I do know, and when I asked you when this was published, this was the point of my question because as I sit here, I ask myself the question, why was it necessary for somebody to publish this in 2001? What purpose might it serve to me, and I do apologise for saying this, but to me it looks like finding an excuse, covering up for something because at that time, 2001, General Pavkovic is the Chief of the General Staff and, of course, he has the right to decide what gets published and what doesn't get published. So if I had seen that at the time, I would probably have told somebody that a criminal report should be filed against the person who provided this data, those data, to be made public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The Vojska is a journal that you can't buy at the newsstand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the part immediately after the heading: "Care for the temporarily displaced Albanian population," you'll see it refers to the plan, and it refers to this being a quotation from the report and conclusions on the implementation of the plan signed by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. So here we have a publication that attributes a report, as do the minutes themselves, to the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. It makes it sound official; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I cannot fully agree with you for the following reason: It is quite apparent that this was published in the Vojska journal because somebody wanted to prove that everything that was done was done the right way, but in the minutes, the document that I was able to read during the break, all those things that General Pavkovic stated, it doesn't say anywhere that he presented this on behalf of the Joint Command. So when you asked me previously, I answered that the Joint Command was never established, nobody ever said that it was established, I never saw any documents, and you can publish or you can write whatever you want in the media, in the press, especially if you're in a position to influence the editorial policy of a paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just have a look at the second page of the minutes where there is the first -- in fact, it's the -- if you look at the third paragraph of the minutes, it starts: "The commander of the Pristina Corps, Pavkovic, gave a brief report ..." And then the next paragraph starts with the words: "Speaking on behalf of the Joint Command ..."

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So there is a clear reference to Pavkovic speaking on behalf of the Joint Command, but I want you to just look at one other item, which is a document from the Government of the Republic of Serbia, P1317. Just read that to yourself. What's your reaction to that document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Complete confusion, Mr. President. So first of all, what you asked me, what you noted, that he said "speaking on behalf of the Joint Command," General Pavkovic, and so on, this is written here; but as I indicated earlier, the minutes, this whole document, does not look real to me. This document, the conclusion that I draw on the basis of this document is that somebody said that this had been done because the author of this document - and there's no signature; there's just the office here -- well, I simply cannot find anything that would convince me that this was how it was. This is all couched in general terms. It says it was established at such and such a date without any specific document, and it functioned in this time-period, and it says according to the knowledge of the military organs. What does it mean? That's not the way that military organs communicate with this office. They draft documents or memos. There should be some kind of a memo that would accompany this. To be quite frank, I'm quite confused with all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, 2002, what was Mr. Pavkovic's position? That's the date the document you have was written.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that at that time he was still the Chief of the General Staff. I'm not sure, but I know that sometime in 2002 or maybe 2003 he was -- he retired. But I think that he was the Chief of the General Staff at that time. Yes, yes, because it says up here, the Federal Ministry of Justice, that's the letterhead, so this is the time when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is still in existence. So as far as I can recall, he was the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you, Mr. Dimitrijevic, aware of meetings that took place in Kosovo, in Pristina, among members of the VJ, members of the MUP, and some of the political figures we discussed earlier under the heading or the general description of Joint Command meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, not under that name. I received information that a certain number of civilians were in Kosovo and that they went to the Pristina Corps command, that they frequented the command. I asked my associates what this was all about, and Lieutenant-Colonel Momir Stojanovic told me that in the evening, during the evening news, some people would get together. He mentioned Sainovic, Minic, Andjelkovic, and Matkovic, and that General Pavkovic, the commander, was also present and that he, Stojanovic, did not attend those meetings. The way he painted this for me was like some kind of informal meetings or some kind of a coordination, and when coordination was mentioned I had this idea in my head that this was coordination between the military and the MUP because he never told me that MUP representatives were coming regularly every evening to attend those meetings. As far as the security administration is concerned, I can say that we never --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, let me interrupt you there. There may be a mistake in the transcript that may be important. You say you had in your head that this was coordination between -- who did you say?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I said coordination of the MUP forces and the military forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you then went on to say you reached that conclusion because he never told you that MUP representatives were coming regularly every evening. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's it, and Stojanovic's explanation was that he did not attend those meetings. And I can say, Mr. President, with full responsibility that not a single document from the security department of the Pristina Corps about those meetings containing the name of the Joint Command ever reached the security administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How often did you speak to Stojanovic about this, or did he speak to you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, not that often, Mr. President. He was the security chief in the corps. In professional terms, his superior was the security chief in the 3rd Army.
