That was Colonel Petar Kuzmanovic; and above them in the professional chain of command, the chain of direction, was the chief of the first department, the operations department. That was for a time Colonel Milinac, and he was then replaced by his deputy Colonel Gajic, so that there were four or five rungs before I was engaged. But I had an opportunity to talk to him over the phone, and I had an opportunity to ask him, Well, what is this whole thing? I hear that there are some civilians there, and this is the reply that I received from him. And I think that I still recall quite clearly what he told me even though ten years have passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did he report to you from time to time on what was happening at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I've already said, Mr. President, that no reports of those meetings ever reached the security administration because Stojanovic explained that he did not attend those meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it fair to say you were interested in what this was all about?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, quite frankly, yes, but after I asked some questions about what was going on, whether this was just an opportunity for them to watch the evening news or whether they discussed anything else, the reply that I received was that Stojanovic did not attend those meetings and that there was nothing for him to report. So the way this was presented to me was some kind of a coordination meeting between the military and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, could I return to some of the collegium minutes we were looking at earlier, and would you have, please, 3D484, and this is the minute of the 10th of December, 1998. Now, about two-thirds of the way through, certainly on page 13 in the English, there is a section attributed to you. It's after -- about a page from General Obradovic, and then you start by referring to him. Now, I wonder if you would go to the last part of your statement there, which starts with the words: "Number three, about the discrepancy between the Pristina Corps, the army, all the way to us here, that's obvious. I think that so many unusual incidents and a lot of what's going on in the Pristina Corps are precisely the consequence of, I am at liberty to say, the alienation of the corps commander and with him the command form the VJ, both from the 3rd Army and the General Staff." Could you tell us more about what was causing you concern?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, when at the collegia meetings of the Chief of General Staff we discussed this, very often in actual fact we didn't know what the real situation was because the operative reports that arrived in the General Staff did not always portray the actual situation as it was. My reactions here have to do with extraordinary events, but I say here at one point by way of a comment that as far as I know the commander -- let me just have a look at the date. Just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the 10th of December.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The commander has already -- 10th of December, yes, yes. The commander has been in Belgrade for two weeks now and that obviously extraordinary events are taking place, and obviously this leads to the commander of the Pristina Corps in a way being alienated or going -- or being above the General Staff in the 3rd Army. In support of that, I can mention the fact that precisely due to a lack of adherence to orders, that is to say he took certain steps on his own, the commander of the 3rd Army at some point towards the end of June started disciplinary proceedings in order to punish Pavkovic because he did not adhere to orders. Unfortunately, once he was given this document stating that disciplinary proceedings were to be instituted against him, I remember full well that a few days after that there was a meeting at President Milosevic's. My conclusion was that there was only one objective involved, that he tell us that things could not be done that way. After a brief discussion on Kosovo, the point was when President Milosevic said, All right, now we are going to have a drink because General Pavkovic has been promoted to the rank of lieutenant-general today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying about certain factual developments, but my question related to the alienation of the corps commander and the command from the VJ, both from the 3rd Army and the General Staff. Now, what were you referring to? It's very difficult to accept that all you meant was he was taking a two-weeks' unauthorised leave in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. As a matter of fact, that's not what I said. I did not say that it was unauthorised leave. I just said that he had been in Belgrade for two weeks then, according to the information that I had. However, in response to your question this is the answer that I wish to give. December is a point in time when General Pavkovic already has direct communication with President Milosevic. When I said this, what I said, alienation, I thought that due to this communication he allowed himself to take certain steps without seeking approval from the army command, or rather, approval from the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you relate that to what you call "so many unusual incidents." What were some of the unusual incidents that led you to conclude that there was direct communication between General Pavkovic and Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, in the military from time to time unusual incidents or extraordinary events were analysed throughout the army. Every army and every corps did this at their own level. There was an annual analysis involved too; however, there were periods when this number would be on the rise. Now, what are these unusual incidents or extraordinary events? It is soldiers who leave unauthorised, who leave guard posts, traffic accidents, deaths, woundings, suicides. In the military -- in a military organization all of these things are extraordinary events or incidents. So when I said direct communication, I did not link that up with this sentence, that he was in Belgrade for already two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in that case let's have clarification. The first sentence I asked you to look at was the one that begins: "Number three, about the discrepancy ..." And then there's the sentence beginning: "I think that so many unusual incidents ..." Would you read that sentence aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: "I think that even this number of unusual incidents and what is happening in the Pristina Corps is a consequence, I'm free to say this in a way, of" -- here it says "of the non-alienation of the corps commander from the Army of Yugoslavia, that is to say from the command of the 3rd Army and the General Staff. Obviously there -- true to the obvious inertia of Kosovo heroes, they can now take it easy." What I meant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, on you go.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: What I meant is that Pavkovic had already secured for himself the role of someone who had resolved the problems in Kosovo, who had become a favourite of the president, if I can put it that way, and who would often say that he is the only one who understands the problems in Kosovo and Metohija and that the General Staff and the people who were sitting in Nis and Belgrade did not understand this and that he is the only one who cares about the Serb people in Kosovo and having them saved and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Dimitrijevic, I don't want to be disrespectful, but if that's what's -- if that's all that's involved, then it sounds as though you were jealous, and it's very difficult sitting here, bearing in mind what we're dealing with, to think that that alone would prompt you to say this at the meeting of the collegium. So please think again and tell us what were the unusual incidents that were leading you to the conclusion that there was disengagement between the high command of the VJ and the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I said what these unusual extraordinary incidents were, soldiers who were fleeing and soldiers who were getting killed, and this was the result of military organization, everything that is called incidents of this kind in an army. I assume that the subject was extraordinary incidents, that this is what General Obradovic had been speaking about before I asked to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But how does that floor --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Further on, further on, if I may, if I may, just one more sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: It is page 12 in the Serbian version where General Obradovic mentions provocations that could take place. That's where I raised this question of what everybody else in the state was doing and how come provocations always come by having the army units attacked, and the reaction follows always after that. What I meant was that the reports about this were not fully truthful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I find it difficult at the moment to understand how the killing of soldiers, or did you say desertion, flows from the commander not obeying his superiors. Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. I wanted to say that extraordinary incidents for the most part take place when discipline in units becomes lax, when soldiers' problems are not dealt with on a day-to-day basis, and usually this lack of discipline results in such tragic events. At that time, soldiers fleeing from the Pristina Corps was a serious problem. If I'm not mistaken, many of them, hundreds of them, were fleeing and trying to get some kind of medical certificates in Belgrade declaring that they were sick so that they could not go back to Kosovo and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what was your understanding of the misreporting or inaccurate information about provocation? Could you explain that more fully, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: My understanding of this is, Mr. President, that whenever the representative of the first administration reported at the collegium of the General Staff where the army was attacked, what was going on down there, invariably when the question would be raised how come something happened, the answer was that some terrorist group had attacked, the unit concerned, the vehicle concerned, the individual concerned, and so on; and then there was a response that followed. So it is for that reason that I put the question a few times as to how it was possible that each and every time we're the ones who are provoked and that it's only then that we resort to force, and rather than -- that this is done in a planned way when one knows with full reliability that every command, every unit, every movement has to be ensured and that every reaction should be appropriate in case of every such attack. That is how I raised these questions. And the second thing was that in another way I also came across some information; for example, through military diplomatic representatives who had access to KLA headquarters and staffs. I remember very well that Mr. Crosland a few -- on a few occasions told me that he saw excessive use of force, as he had put it. I also remember very well that I asked him a few times that he document this for me in some way so that I could deal with it at the collegium of the Chief of General Staff, that I could raise the question quite openly, what was being done. Regrettably, I never got anything from him, although I had received promises that I would get video cassettes or whatever, some other material. So it is for all these reasons that I came to this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If I can go back to the first reason, the questions you raised about why events occurred as a result of provocation by the KLA. What answers did you get to these questions?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, almost regularly the representative of the operative administration or the assistant Chief of General Staff for operations in staff, General Obradovic, almost regularly replied that we received this report from the Pristina command, the 3rd Army, through regular channels, and that that was written in those reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you satisfied with that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that I wasn't and the Chief of General Staff wasn't because at one point, as a matter of fact, he ordered that he be provided with daily information about ammunition spent because information was coming in that nothing was being done and ammunition was nevertheless being spent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you referring to General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Afterwards, too, in December, General Ojdanic as Chief of General Staff also put the question of the use of ammunition and the accuracy of reports received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, can we move to the next of these that I want to ask you about, 3D494, and this is the minute of the 17th of December. And in this one, in English I have you commenting at page 19, and it's immediately after a very short question from General Ojdanic, and there you're saying, stressing that the VJ should deal with things assigned by the constitution, namely, the protection of the border. And you say: "Neither the corps commander nor the army commander can keep on telling us that they have undertaken everything while at the same time the forces in the field are growing. We will again be blamed for that." And you go on to say that "The army should be concentrating on closing the border creating preconditions for the MUP to resolve other problems because this is not the army's task." Now, what was it that was happening that you did not think should be happening?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, after I spoke with regard to this question what the proposals were, the question put by General Ojdanic, I said what is written here. The basic thing was to shut the border, not to allow weapons to come in and to have terrorists who were trained in Albania enter our territory, carry out actions, and have that kind of thing spread, quite simply. Practically, the MUP kept accusing us all the time - when I say "us," I mean the military - that they, lo and behold, cannot carry out their tasks because the number of terrorists is going up all the time; their weapons are on the rise, as well, because the military are not securing the border properly. So that is why at these collegium meetings I kept repeating that the border and its shutting or closing down is something that should be done by the army primarily, and that's why I thought it's not a good thing for the army commander or the corps commander to say to us that they have done everything and on the other hand the terrorist forces are on the rise. That is why I repeated this proposal, that basically measures should be taken to close the border down as much as possible, to a maximum, and to prevent people from being brought in and ammunition and weapons; and in this way conditions would be created for anti-terrorist actions to be carried out by the MUP and to deal with the terrorists in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for that, but I was really anxious to know what the army was doing if it wasn't closing the border. How was it spending its time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, that is why I was putting these questions at the collegium and issuing these warnings because obviously what was happening was that at that time we had lots of these groups that tried to enter the territory of Kosovo from Albania. A patrol of the army would stop such a group, and this group of terrorists would come in, and I remember this one particular case - I can't remember the name right now, of course - but this was a lieutenant who was head of a patrol, and a group of terrorists passed by him. I remember that I ordered straight away that criminal charges be filed, that the lieutenant be detained, but I also remember that nothing came out of it because someone protected him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was your complaint about?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not that I complained, but I'm saying that what happened was that in spite of all the measures taken, the leader of a patrol or someone who was at the border itself would allow a group to get in. And I remember one case when criminal charges were brought against an officer who let that happen, but nothing came out of it ultimately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move, then, to P928, which is the 30th of December. It's page 14 in the English I'm looking at, and you speak after a long passage from General Marjanovic and before General Obradovic. And about seven or eight lines, maybe a little more, into what you say you turn to the situation in the vicinity of Podujevo, and you refer to the so-called pretend or real planned exercises in which this company took part in the field. And you say to General Ojdanic: "These sorts of moves will lead us to disaster. The explanation that this was a planned exercise, that is not true. It was planned that the unit would provoke the terrorists so that the MUP would then have to do whatever it had to do." Can you amplify that for us, please, what was happening or what had happened in that situation?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't remember these details, that is to say in this specific case. But it is quite possible - I mean, I'm not challenging that this was my reaction - or perhaps I had information -- actually, I know that soon after this things were checked, and General Obradovic explained that after an additional report was requested they established that, after all, this was not a provocation; rather, this was a planned exercise. My reaction came precisely because there was something planned all the time, and what happened after that would happen. I think that one of our officers or soldiers got killed on that occasion or wounded, and that was the reason we discussed this at the collegium. However, if I'm not mistaken - and I don't have time now to read this in great detail - I think that the then-Chief of General Staff, that is to say General Ojdanic, said that he was asking for this to be checked, and he was saying that he should be informed about this. There is no reason not to know whether things were that way or were not that way. I just found the part where General Dragoljub Ojdanic is speaking, and he says here: "As for the assertions made here that with regard to the situation in Podujevo what was caused was the presence of this unit, and the only question was whether their marching orders were right in terms of the location that they were supposed to be at. They were, indeed, in camp. So they -- so he, rather, checked this, and he also mentioned the withdrawal of some groups. So what was controversial there? After all, he as Chief of General Staff admits that too. The question was whether the marching orders were right and whether the route was right and so on. And I think at this collegium I think that he and I were involved in a bit of a polemic, how we would plan this had it been the two of us on the move, if that is what we are talking about here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They're quite strong words you use, Mr. Dimitrijevic, the explanation that "This was a planned exercise is not true. It was planned that the unit would provoke the terrorists so that the MUP would then have to do whatever it had to do." And I don't think I see a withdrawal of these remarks anywhere. Are you saying that you got it wrong?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think I got it wrong. I think that later this was checked and that it was precisely Obradovic who explained later during the course of this collegium meeting that they checked this and that that was that; and I see here that the chief of the operations team speaks at the beginning of the collegium that in the village of Obrandza, a lieutenant and a soldier from the 15th Brigade were wounded and so on and so forth, and that was the reason why this topic was discussed a bit more at this collegium meeting. So in view of these contacts that I had and in view of the different soldiers of information that I had, probably I had a basis for saying this. I used that to issue a warning saying that such things would definitely have negative consequences for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have to break again at this stage, Mr. Dimitrijevic. We'll break on this occasion for 20 minutes and resume just after ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, there is one further point from these minutes I want to ask you about. Yes, there's an earlier part of the minutes where you speak at greater length. It's up to page 9 in the English, and it's towards the end of what you say. You're speaking just before General Ojdanic says something quite brief, if you can find that part, and you are concerned about increased terrorist activity, and you say: "It's realistic to expect the security situation in Kosovo to become even more complex. This leading question characterized by the brutality of terrorist acts and the overall uncertainty and fear of Serbs and Montenegrins which could result in extreme," and there's something missing, "with perhaps deliberate intention on the part of individuals to take advantage in an increased number of people leaving or taking counter measures difficult to control." And then you say: "When I say 'counter measures,' I'm thinking about a figure of about 60.000 armed Serbs that can be mobilised outside the control of the official organs." Now, who are these 60.000 armed Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think that in this case -- well, there's note that they may be mobilised. So I'm expressing the concern that perhaps some individuals or groups might abuse the fact that terrorist acts and general insecurity and the atmosphere of fear would be present in the villages where Serbs lived. So when it comes to this, a certain number of persons were armed, both by the military and by the MUP at an earlier stage; and I think that by the decision of the 3rd Army commander a certain number of Serbs, Montenegrins, and -- well, non-Albanians in general were armed. That was a contingency against a pogrom being perpetrated against them by those forces, and here also I am referring to the reserve force of the MUP, too, because at those meetings, at those presentations, reference was always made that the reserve force of the MUP should receive weapons so that if there was an escalation those people could be mobilised and used. As far as the military is concerned, as far as I can remember, an order was issued by the army to assign personnel, commanders, who would be put in charge of making sure that weapons would not end up being abused or misused. And as far as I can recall, we didn't have any cases where civilians misused the weapons they had been issued with; in other words, I'm talking about them using weapons for any other purpose. It simply served to protect those people against any terrorist acts. That was the purpose of those weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could I ask you to look, please, at P939, which relates to the meeting of the 21st of January.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, that's the 24th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: If that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think I have the wrong number on mine. Just a second. No, the 24th of December should be 924. Look, please, at 939, which is the 21st of January. It has a date, 24th December, at the bottom, but it's actually minutes for the 21st of January.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. I saw what was written at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I am interested in certain information about Racak in this document. The Chamber is not interested in the -- investigating the detail of the action within the village, if any. Now, on page 9 in the English you speak after a short intervention by General Panic and before General Obradovic, and you asked the question: "Was the army engaged or not?" And then there's a short --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's then an answer about an exercise involving the 8th Federal Mechanised Tank Squad, and then you say a part of the 243rd Combat Group was also carrying out an exercise. It also said "planned exercise." Now, you appear to have been concerned about the circumstances in which units of the VJ came to be involved in the area. What was your concern?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, unlike the previous cases, I have a very good recollection of this one. After Racak, a presidential press release was issued stating that the action in Racak was carried out by the MUP together with the army. At the collegium meeting, I raised the question whether this was, in fact, true, whether the army really had taken part in this action. From all the military diplomatic representatives, we got the same response that an investigation was underway to determine whether the army had participated in the action or not. The OSCE Verification Mission was also doing that, and there was a presidential statement from the Security Council indicating quite clearly that the army did take part, and my question was aimed at the Chief of the General Staff. I asked him whether he could tell us, all of us, the whole collegium whether he had the actual correct information to the effect that the army participated in the action or not. And I think that his response was something along the lines that this was not in any reports; in other words, that the army did not take part. And I think that I pressed the point, and he ordered at that meeting that a wire should be sent through the operation and staff department requesting that the commander of the corps - at that time it was General Pavkovic - make a specific statement answering whether the army was involved in this action or not. And I think that after a second or a third check, the response was always received that the army did not participate in the action. That led me to issue a statement that the army did not participate in that, that it was being blamed for no reason, but every time some excuses were made to the effect that we should not really make any statements, I think that Krga, I can see now that Krga says at this meeting that he heard from some military attache that the artillery had been active in this area. So the answers from the corps were all to the effect that the army did not participate. And through my associates, I insisted on receiving an answer from the security people down the security chain of command, and I wanted Colonel Stojanovic to give us an answer, what he knew as the security chief about any involvement of the army in this. And if I recall correctly -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is it fair to say General Ojdanic didn't know the answer?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think you could say that he did not know the answer and that he accepted my proposal that another wire telegram be sent asking Pavkovic to clearly state whether the army had been involved or not. And the finale was that perhaps a couple of platoons [as interpreted] were involved to provide transportation for the MUP units, something like that, if I'm not mistaken. But at any rate, ten years have passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, let's -- just go to the point after Krga that you referred to, and you'll see that General Ojdanic speaking. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. Transcript 64, 16; I believe the witness said couple of vehicles and not platoons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Couple of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. 63, 16. Yeah. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters do apologise. We would like to note that there is a echo and that leads to us not hearing things properly. The two words in B/C/S are very similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it you're not saying there was one vehicle and the other one was an echo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, what I said was -- no, no, I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's okay. It's unboardly of me. Now, General Ojdanic is speaking. If you go to the second paragraph of what he says, he talks about this joint staff command or whatever decided that the operation in Racak village "could not be carried out without the assistance of the Yugoslav Army. We know very well who must be asked for approval." Now, do you know what that is a reference to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, it says here that this action against the village of Racak -- that's what it says. This is all about this incident in Racak. But it may be an error in translation, but in line 2 General Ojdanic says -- but this means that if this joint -- or whatever. So he himself does not have a clear position; he doesn't say what he really means. He says "concluded," not "decided," that this action could not be carried out without support from the army. So he says quite appropriately that it is quite well-known who can order that, the president or the Supreme Defence Council; and if this order is issued, this decision must be implemented. But in light of the restrictions that stem from the Holbrooke Agreement, he does not have the right to do that. In that case, this should have come from above, from the president through the Chief of General Staff down to the army commander and all the way down to General Pavkovic. And in second paragraph, if you will allow me, he says precisely what I myself said a few minutes ago. In addition to the oral order and the report that is received, at my request after contacting the military representatives he is asking for an answer about all this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We understand that --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: -- because this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We understand that --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: -- was an event that was quite important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, we understand that these inquiries were initiated. What I'm trying to understand is the reference to the joint whichever it was, but to help me understand it perhaps you can explain what was in the Holbrooke Agreement that created restrictions on the actions of Ojdanic or Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I don't recall the details of the agreement, so there are several papers that were signed at that time. So if you're talking about the military part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: -- the part that was done with General Clark in the General Staff, I can talk about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is you that's raised it, and you mentioned the Holbrooke Agreement in the context of reading out the reference there to the restrictions contained in the agreement. Now, what is it you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this agreement, in light of the fact that the units of the Yugoslav Army, of the Pristina Corps were for the most part outside of their barracks, the agreement called for all the units of the Pristina Corps to go back to their original garrisons. Second, that all the units that had been brought to the Kosovo rim from other strategic groups that are not part of the Pristina Corps in accordance with the establishment, that they should also return to their original garrisons. So this agreement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I follow what you're saying now. So can you help me, then, by reading that first sentence that you referred to, that's "if the forces have to be used, no one is denying ..." Could you read that aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: My sentence, what I said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. What Ojdanic says. It's actually the second sentence of that whole section: "If the forces have to be used, nobody is denying that right ..." Just read it aloud for us, please, so that it can be translated into English.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, let me find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the section which you say refers also to the Holbrooke Agreement. After General Krga, you've then got the reference of what Ojdanic says, and it's the second paragraph of that. If you just read the beginning of it, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I found it. Yes. "If the forces have to be used, nobody is denying that right to those who have the right to order it, but what it means is that if this joint staff, command, or whatever it is decided that the operation in the Racak village cannot be carried out without the assistance of the Army of Yugoslavia" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's fine. Stop there. Now, what is the joint staff, command, or whatever to which he is referring?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I really can't say what this reference is to, but it is quite clear that he was confused about what he meant, whether he meant the coordination staff that we were told existed or anything else. I really can't tell you what he was referring to because he did not specifically say combined staff or command, "zdruzeni" staff or "komanda." I really can't tell you what he meant by that, and I wouldn't like to speculate here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Doesn't it look like some body that can bypass General Ojdanic and go directly to the president?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. It might be a reference to some body, but it might be also a reference to the fact that there was a direct line of communication leading from Pavkovic to the president. So I don't know who concluded that this action could not be carried out, whether it was Pavkovic or whoever it was representing the MUP, whether they sat down, analysed the situation, and concluded that. I really can't tell you that. I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can I ask you to look at one for the 2nd of February, which is P931, and this time I'm looking at page 18 in the English where you speak after General Samardzic and before General Borovic. And at that stage, it's known that there are to be negotiations about the future of Kosovo; indeed, there are negotiations ongoing, and you say something about what the politicians intend to do. Do you have that part?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I just found it. Yes, I'm reading it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you read aloud the first sentence of what you said there.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. "In my opinion, it is not good for the General Staff to try to guess what the state solution is. We have a state; we have the supreme commander, and surely they should say what the army should do in order to act in accordance with what the politicians intend to do."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was your concern in saying that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, most likely, Mr. President, because we didn't know anything, we didn't have any decisions about what would happen if the negotiations succeed, partially succeed, or fall through. So I advocated the approach whereby the state should bear its part of the responsibility. So the supreme commander, the Supreme Defence Council, should make a decision, prepare the army for such and such option, and it was General Samardzic's proposal to do that because as Samardzic says, if the negotiations fall through we know that the carrot and stick approach --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to read more slowly. The interpreters cannot keep up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is why I responded in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think that's adequate for this answer. The interpreters are telling us that you're speaking rather quickly for them. If you can possibly speak a little more slowly, that would help. Now, did you ever have occasion to attend meetings of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, never, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've heard some evidence that when it came to a war, the Supreme Defence Council name may have changed. Is that your experience?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I assume that you're asking me about something that was already regulated by the rules. So the Supreme Defence Council did not change its name in wartime, unlike in peacetime, so in peacetime the Supreme Defence Council is in command of the army and deals with all the other issues. In the war there is the supreme commander; that was the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the Supreme Defence Council no longer exists in wartime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: -- so the Supreme Command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just in case anyone's concerned that I'm simply accepting what you say, it's sufficient for present purposes. I say to you that's not consistent with the evidence we have in the case, and we'll have to review all the evidence before deciding what the overall picture is. But the reason I mention it at this stage is because you use the expression "supreme commander" in the comment you've made in the minutes, and you use it in a time of peace. So is that just loose use of language, or is there something else behind it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: In an error but -- or a lapse, but the situation was such that it was not difficult to guess who the reference is to here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what we do know a bit more clearly is that when war occurred, the General Staff had a different title; is that your understanding of the position?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the rules, it said that in the war the General Staff becomes the Supreme Command Staff. So in wartime, the Supreme Command comprises the president with his advisors and associates; and the Supreme Command Staff is an integral part of the Supreme Command. So the president as the supreme commander making all the decisions and the staff that actually operationalises his decisions by turning them into orders, plans, and other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may not be aware of rules that were passed on the 23rd of March about the Supreme Defence Council, which may lead you to a different view, but we don't need to explore that at the moment. What I would like to know is whether the Supreme Command Staff was in any way significantly different from the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know -- actually, Mr. President, first of all I wish to say that on the 23rd of March I was definitely excluded from the General Staff; secondly, I also have to say to you that already before that, from the end of December onwards, I was on ice, so to speak, because I was expected to leave that position, probably because I was constantly saying certain things, cautioning about this and that and so on. Of course this has nothing to do with this question. I'm not aware of the document that was adopted on the 23rd of March because by then I was no longer there. I assume that the General Staff remained the same, or rather, in accordance with the rules and regulations, part was with the supreme commander, and another part was at some forward -- at some command post, and a third section was somewhere else. So basically, during the war the General Staff was simply called something different, the supreme defence staff, and -- Supreme Command Staff, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could we turn to the minutes of the 4th of February, P932. Now, in this case, in the English version you're recorded as speaking at page 5, 6, and into page 7, and I'm concerned about page 7, the end of what you say before General Ojdanic speaks briefly. And you say there that "34 telephones in the command of the Pristina Corps, including that of its commander, are being wire-tapped by state security. I'm asking you if someone has ordered the army to be controlled, what the purpose of this is." And you go on to say that there are moves to replace you and to appoint a new chief of the administration, which is a different post from yours. Now, you're then asked if you can prove any of -- prove the wire-tapping, and you say that you've got proof for every single word you've said. Now, what did you understand was happening?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, everything I said, I said at the collegium precisely so that all members of the collegium would be aware of that. I said what had been revealed by the security organs, and this was an undeniable fact that later on in the presence of the Chief of General Staff and the then-state of security I proved that to the president at his office with documents, or rather, photographs. It is correct that all telephones, all military telephones, were wire-tapped at the command of the Pristina Corps. It is correct that this was done by the State Security Service. Now, whether this was supposed to control the army, I personally think that that was the case. When we went with General Ojdanic, because he made this possible for me, I asked at this collegium - I think that Ojdanic said that he was not competent - I asked for a meeting with the president, and we went together, both Ojdanic and I; a few days later we went, and I said all of that to President Milosevic. Of course, he expressed his surprise, disbelief. He called the then-chief of the state security Rade Markovic. He told me what he had heard from me, and he decided something that I was 100 per cent sure in advance that he would do, that a Joint Commission be established, that would go to the actual location involved, that would overview the situation and say whether this was wire-tapping or not. Of course, this was done -- or it was done a few days later; and after that, yet another meeting took place at Milosevic's office - however, it was not attended by Ojdanic - where I proved to him that there, indeed, had been wire-tapping. As a matter of fact, I remember very well that I said the following sentence: Mr. President, is this being done with your knowledge or without your knowledge? Because if it is done with your knowledge, that proves that you do not trust the army; if it's being done without your knowledge, then you should give this some thought, where you are in all of this. After that, he told me that I could leave. He stayed with Markovic, and that was the end of that. Roughly, all of those -- during the course of all of those days, I was asking [as interpreted] to be called in and told that I was no longer head of the service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've been translated as saying you were asking to be called in and told you were no longer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter said "waiting."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Waiting. Sorry. You were waiting to be called in. Yeah, thank you. And can I take you now to the 25th of February, and that's P941. Now, in this -- this is again a meeting that you attended, and I would like you to look at page 24 in the English where General Ojdanic is speaking. Now, do you have that part, Mr. Dimitrijevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: May I ask what it pertains to exactly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. The part I'm concerned about is in the middle of the English, page 24, where you are referred to by Ojdanic and, it's to do with an anti-terrorist battalion being introduced into Kosovo when it should not have been. And it's your objection to this course of action that is being supported by General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, obviously that was my reaction because I was not aware that the battalion for anti-terrorist activity, that basically is a military police unit from the 72nd Special Brigade, is being sent to the area of Kosovo and Metohija. That is when I expressed my dissatisfaction, and I protested why this was being done without anyone asking anything. Of course, I reacted to General Curcin and Obradovic, as well, because they're the ones who wrote that order; but this order probably came from the Chief of General Staff. So my reaction was - and I think that it was quite justified at that point in time - because I was afraid that this unit would not be used properly. The anti-terrorist battalion is an exceptionally strong unit, and I believe that at that point in time it was one of the strongest military police units. That is to say, I saw no reason for it to go down there except to help that the 52nd Battalion, which I think was somewhere around Lake Radonjic, that it be allowed to rest a bit because people were exhausted by then. People in the administration who were in charge of military police were telling me about this. I think it was not right for that unit to go and to replace the battalion that was in that area. And the other reason why I reacted was because I assumed - and I think that that proved to be correct later - that the unit would not remain there as a whole, that it would be crumbled, so to speak, in smaller parts, and then it wouldn't be used properly. Regrettably, that proved to be the case later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, in the next paragraph after the reference to this, General Ojdanic in the middle of that next paragraph refers to a state being proclaimed. Do you see that part? The paragraph begins: "The fragmentation of units is a very bad practice ..." And then about halfway through, just over halfway through, it says: "Internally, if a state is proclaimed ..." So he's expressing the view that you did about fragmentation. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I haven't found it. On what page is that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, I'm sorry. I'm giving you the English page. It's page 24 in English and --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: You must tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's about one page --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: So page 24 in English. In Serbian ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's page 23 in the B/C/S, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Page 23 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, do you see the reference in the middle of the page --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... seem to find it, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- to fragmentation and Marjanovic and then halfway through that paragraph: " ... if a state is proclaimed, both our and MUP forces, only we will be spearheading combat operations, but no one can relieve us of the duty regarding the state border ..." Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was General Ojdanic referring to when he said "if a state is proclaimed"?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was quite certain that if there is an escalation of terrorism and if a state of emergency is proclaimed or a state of emergency in part of the territory or a state of war, I think that is what he was referring to, one of those states. But then in the further text, it says that we, the army, are going to be the protagonists of military activities or combat operations. I believe that there is no dilemma there. He meant if a state of war is proclaimed or declared, but then again he repeats in that same sentence: "However, no one can free us as far as the state border is concerned" and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: That is what I kept --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the significance of the army and the use of the army of declaring a state of emergency or of a state of war arising?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in case a state of emergency is declared, the army is issued with a task. It is the organizer and protagonist of all activities in the territory where the state of emergency is declared, starting with an imposition of a curfew and including all other activities in which the MUP takes part, as well, but all of it is under the army, that is to say that then the civilians, the state authority --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was it --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: -- carries out tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did declaring a state of emergency have significance for the area of operation of the army? In other words, could it operate throughout the territory to which the state of emergency applied?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if a state of emergency were to be declared in part of the territory, then the army would operate within that part of the territory. That does not mean that a state of emergency would apply to the rest of the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was there a point in 1998 when you were concerned that the correct course of action for the president to have taken would have been to declare a state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, Mr. President, we heard explanations to the effect that it's not good because of the world and so on and so forth, and there was insistence all the time that the army was supposed to do things that were not within its domain of work. So for those reasons, I was in favour of declaring a certain state of emergency in part of the territory because things would be clearest in that way and then engage the army in that way, not to engage it ad hoc on the basis of decisions made by the president without foundation in laws and regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were there other senior army officers who supported that view?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think, Mr. President, as far as the General Staff level is concerned that a majority were in favour of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you look now at the next paragraph, you'll see the issue being addressed there is unauthorised mobilisation. Can you assist us by telling us what that related to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously, this is a reaction on the part of General Ojdanic to the information provided by the late General Risto Matovic, the then-assistant chief for personnel and mobilisation affairs. Probably, Matovic was saying that thousands of people were being called up from the reserve and that that had not been agreed upon because the order was that things should go up to the quota that had been approved. Now, this pertains to the 3rd Army and General Pavkovic because Ojdanic says further on: "I don't want to make any further comments, just draw attention" -- "Pavkovic's attention to this," and so on and so forth. So they called up a larger number without that having been approved by the General Staff. That is how I see it now, at least on the basis of what is written here. If you allow me, Mr. President, on one of the previous pages - in Serbian it's page 15 - there is a part where General Risto Matovic is speaking, and he says how some of the soldiers whose term is coming to an end, how they can be kept longer in the army and with that being legal. And then he also talks about the reservists who were called up and in view of how much this costs, per diems, et cetera, that it was a lot more than had been originally allocated. And it is on the basis of that that the Chief of General Staff spoke and his conclusion, namely, that Pavkovic was cautioned that that is not the way things were supposed to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, could I ask you to look at P933. That's the 4th of March, page 15 in English. It would help if someone can tell me the B/C/S page reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If it's the part where General Dimitrijevic is speaking, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- that's B -- that's page 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Page 13, Mr. Dimitrijevic. Now, there you're talking about reports of attacks on the army, and in the third paragraph, you say: "Why should we tolerate it that every morning I regularly read combat reports which say everywhere precisely that a unit has been attacked? I mean, we should not allow them to continue to tell us lies because in the end it will end up at the door of the General Staff." Now, is this just a continuation of what we saw earlier when you expressed a similar view at the time of the Podujevo incident?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was it throughout --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you consider this to be a problem throughout 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, already in March 1999 I had left the military, so in that period --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I simply mean up until the 23rd of March.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think the answer is yes, and at quite a few of these collegiums this question was raised in terms of checking reports, and the Chief of General Staff was commenting on this, and he was angry because he did not have full and accurate information as to what was happening in the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And if you look now at P938 and go to the English, page 21, which going by past form might be 19 in B/C/S. Do you see there a reference to things you said, again, about attacks on army units?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I've already said that. Practically at every collegium meeting, in a way I raised the issue and voiced my criticism as to why measures were not being taken down the chain of command so that we really know what is going on. This question was addressed to General Curcin. At that time, he was there on behalf of the first administration, the operative administration, and my reaction was, as is stated here -- of course, I don't recall all of these details, but as it is written here, it looks like what my usual reactions were. 16 attacks against army units during the course of the week, and I'm saying whether a single one of these actions was done on the basis of us carrying out this action in a planned fashion or where we invariably attacked first. Indeed, most sincerely, Mr. President, I was trying to help the Chief of General Staff so that he would have the right things at hand. Sometimes I spoke in too strong terms. How is it possible that the Chief of General Staff doesn't know certain things, how he is going to respond if somebody puts questions to him, and of course, I realize that his answers would not be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And now please go to a little earlier in that minute to page 11 in the English - that may be 10 in B/C/S - and there's a lengthy account of you speaking over about three pages.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And if you go --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the regular assessment I presented every week about the security situation, not only in Kosovo but in the territory and in the army, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, if you go about a page into that, you'll see reference to the theory that the MUP and the army are conducting mopping-up operations of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's just over halfway down on page 9 in the B/C/S, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Page 9, halfway, Mr. Dimitrijevic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's, again, reference to the attacks on the army, but you'll see there the theory that the MUP and the army are conducting mopping-up operations. Now, what was --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What concerned you about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: That is what I stated there unequivocally. We had a great deal of information to the effect that in the west there is a thesis that is omnipresent. That is what I'm saying here, that in the west there is lots of information to the effect that territory -- mopping-up operations are taking place in the territory. Every morning, I read combat reports of the Pristina Corps, and not in a single case did I find a situation that we were conducting something. Instead, it was always them - I meant the terrorists - who were attacking us, and we would respond. So information was coming in from many sides, and reports from the corps stated that we weren't doing anything anywhere. Only when a unit or someone was attacked, there would be a response and nothing more than that. And further on, if you allow me, I read the next paragraph, and I propose here that at the General Staff level, at least, even if not everyone should know everything, I think that the Chief of General Staff, who is a personification of the army as an institution, as a whole, at least he should know the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You used the expression "mopping-up operations." Was that an expression that caused you any concern?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No. What caused my concern was the fact that we had already enough experience, that every time an argument was put forward by the military diplomatic representatives from the west, we would always end up being blamed, being the guilty party, and that is why I say that they put forward this argument that we are conducting mop-up operations. And since there was no mention of that in any of the reports, I here reacted by warning the Chief of the General Staff that -- we're talking about the 18th of March. That's five days before I left the army. At that time, I was already distancing myself from all those problems, but I'm warning in good faith the General Staff that he should -- the Chief of the General Staff that he should be aware of that because it would be an ugly situation if he were to be found out not knowing about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have to interrupt your evidence at this stage, Mr. Dimitrijevic, for the evening. We cannot continue beyond 7.00. Just let me check one thing first of all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That means, Mr. Dimitrijevic, we will resume at 2.15 tomorrow, same arrangements as today. You need to be in the office where you are in good time to start at 2.15. Please bear in mind - and this is vital - that between now and then, it is absolutely fundamental rule of our procedure that you must not communicate with anybody about the evidence in this case. That doesn't interrupt your normal routine way of living, but whatever else you talk about to people you must not have any communication, discussion of any nature about the evidence in the case. We'll now switch off the video conference link, and you are free to leave the office and return there at -- for 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It follows from what's happened today that the order requiring submission of final briefs today is suspended until we get to a stage where we can determine when to require these briefs. Can I have some indication from any parties of the time they would like to occupy realistically?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I advise you of that tomorrow or by e-mail later after consulting with my colleagues? This witness covers a lot of territory. It impacts on a lot of areas in our brief. It's hard for me to predict right now on my feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Whatever I do tomorrow, I will not occupy more than one session, and I'm keen to try to limit that. We've been very selective about the things that have been asked, and everyone has to follow that course, but obviously if we've raised issues that require to be explored, then we cannot prevent you from doing that. But we invite you to be very selective in any additional areas that you seek to explore. The Defence, also, is there anyone there who can give me any indication of what's likely to be insisted upon so far as you can? Silence. I do remember that with Mr. Djakovic there wasn't extensive examination by parties. That was appreciated in the circumstances -- maybe it wasn't necessary, and maybe it's more necessary here. It's difficult for me to judge that. All right. Well, I will try to finish as quickly as possible, but I could take up to one more session tomorrow, and we'll assess the situation at that stage with the aim of completing the evidence tomorrow. There is the possibility of some additional time but not very much at a later stage in the week, and obviously from the point of view of the health of the witness, it would be desirable to avoid that if we can. But if need be, then we will use it. So we will now adjourn until 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
